The Euler Product

A series gets sieved until only the primes remain. The sum turns out to equal a product over all primes.

Multiply by the factor that erases the even terms, and the evens vanish. Multiply by the factor for multiples of 3, and those vanish too. Sieve once for each prime and only prime information survives. Even the product over the first few primes already lands close to the answer.

For example, line up 🍬 candies numbered from 1 onward. Remove the even numbers, then the multiples of 3, and only prime numbers stay. This sieving is what builds the product formula.

ζ(s)=∑n=1∞1ns=∏p prime11−p−s(s>1)\zeta(s) = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^s} = \prod_{p\ \mathrm{prime}}\frac{1}{1-p^{-s}} \qquad (s > 1)ζ(s)=n=1∑∞​ns1​=p prime∏​1−p−s1​(s>1)
∏p11−p−2=π26\prod_p\frac{1}{1-p^{-2}} = \frac{\pi^2}{6}p∏​1−p−21​=6π2​

log⁡ζ(s)=∑p∑j≥11j pjs=∑p1ps+O(1)(s>1)\log \zeta(s) = \sum_{p}\sum_{j\ge 1} \frac{1}{j\,p^{js}} = \sum_{p} \frac{1}{p^s} + O(1) \qquad (s > 1)logζ(s)=p∑​j≥1∑​jpjs1​=p∑​ps1​+O(1)(s>1)

Show proof

  1. Justify taking logs for s>1s > 1s>1: for a finite partial product, log⁡\loglog turns the product into a sum of logs; the partial products converge to ζ(s)>0\zeta(s) > 0ζ(s)>0, so continuity of log⁡\loglog passes this to the limit.

    Using −log⁡(1−x)=∑j≥1xjj-\log(1 - x) = \sum_{j\ge 1} \frac{x^j}{j}−log(1−x)=∑j≥1​jxj​ (Taylor series, ∣x∣<1|x| < 1∣x∣<1) gives log⁡ζ(s)=∑p∑j≥11j pjs\log \zeta(s) = \sum_{p}\sum_{j\ge 1} \frac{1}{j\,p^{js}}logζ(s)=∑p​∑j≥1​jpjs1​.

    Every term 1j pjs\frac{1}{j\,p^{js}}jpjs1​ is positive, so Tonelli's theorem for counting measure permits any rearrangement of the double sum, and the double sum converges absolutely for s>1s > 1s>1.

    Splitting off j=1j = 1j=1 yields log⁡ζ(s)=∑p1ps+∑p∑j≥21j pjs\log \zeta(s) = \sum_{p} \frac{1}{p^s} + \sum_{p}\sum_{j\ge 2} \frac{1}{j\,p^{js}}logζ(s)=∑p​ps1​+∑p​∑j≥2​jpjs1​.

  2. The j≥2j \ge 2j≥2 double sum is uniformly bounded for s≥1s \ge 1s≥1: ∑p∑j≥21j pjs≤∑p1p2∑j≥221−j=∑p1p2<∑n≥21n2=ζ(2)−1=π26−1≈0.6449341\sum_{p}\sum_{j\ge 2} \frac{1}{j\,p^{js}} \le \sum_{p} \frac{1}{p^2}\sum_{j\ge 2} 2^{1-j} = \sum_{p} \frac{1}{p^2} < \sum_{n\ge 2} \frac{1}{n^2} = \zeta(2) - 1 = \frac{\pi^2}{6} - 1 \approx 0.6449341∑p​∑j≥2​jpjs1​≤∑p​p21​∑j≥2​21−j=∑p​p21​<∑n≥2​n21​=ζ(2)−1=6π2​−1≈0.6449341, so that part is O(1)O(1)O(1). Hence log⁡ζ(s)=∑p1ps+O(1)\log \zeta(s) = \sum_{p} \frac{1}{p^s} + O(1)logζ(s)=∑p​ps1​+O(1) for s>1s > 1s>1.

  3. Meanwhile ζ(s)≥∫1∞x−s dx=1s−1\zeta(s) \ge \int_1^{\infty} x^{-s}\,dx = \frac{1}{s-1}ζ(s)≥∫1∞​x−sdx=s−11​ — just sum n−s≥∫nn+1x−s dxn^{-s} \ge \int_n^{n+1} x^{-s}\,dxn−s≥∫nn+1​x−sdx over nnn. Hence log⁡ζ(s)≥−log⁡(s−1)→+∞\log \zeta(s) \ge -\log(s - 1) \to +\inftylogζ(s)≥−log(s−1)→+∞ as s→1+s \to 1^+s→1+.

  4. Since log⁡ζ(s)=∑pp−s+O(1)→+∞\log \zeta(s) = \sum_{p} p^{-s} + O(1) \to +\inftylogζ(s)=∑p​p−s+O(1)→+∞, we get ∑pp−s→+∞\sum_{p} p^{-s} \to +\infty∑p​p−s→+∞ as s→1+s \to 1^+s→1+.

    Set up the monotone convergence step: for each prime ppp, p−sp^{-s}p−s increases to p−1p^{-1}p−1 as s↓1s \downarrow 1s↓1, and every term is nonnegative, so the monotone convergence theorem for counting measure gives ∑pp−s↑∑pp−1\sum_{p} p^{-s} \uparrow \sum_{p} p^{-1}∑p​p−s↑∑p​p−1 as s→1+s \to 1^+s→1+ (the limit may be +∞+\infty+∞).

    Hence if ∑p1p\sum_{p} \frac{1}{p}∑p​p1​ converged to a finite value at s=1s = 1s=1, ∑pp−s\sum_{p} p^{-s}∑p​p−s would have to approach that sum as s→1+s \to 1^+s→1+ — a contradiction.

    Therefore ∑p1p=+∞\sum_{p} \frac{1}{p} = +\infty∑p​p1​=+∞: the sum of prime reciprocals diverges.
